teaching_path.action: List the supplied local inventories beside equivalence.
teaching_path.why_valid: CO2 C has two domains; nitrate N three; NH3 N four although each case has equivalent central bonds.
inputs: For the benchmark, use these supplied simplified observations, not an exam-source claim: CO2 is linear with two equivalent C–O bonds; NO3− is planar with three equivalent N–O bonds; NH3 is pyramidal with three equivalent N–H bonds. Assess the claim 'Equivalent bonds imply sp2 at the central atom.' Use counterexamples and valid warrants, and distinguish equivalence, electron-domain count and hybridisation as a model description.
teaching_path.output: Two, three and four local totals with equivalence held true.

teaching_path.action: Use CO2 or NH3 as a counterexample.
teaching_path.why_valid: One case satisfying the premise but failing the claimed sp2 consequence refutes a universal implication.
inputs: Two, three and four local totals with equivalence held true.
teaching_path.output: CO2 uses introductory sp; NH3 sp3-like; the claim is false.

teaching_path.action: Separate model labels from observable bond equality.
teaching_path.why_valid: Domain count and orbital allocation are different layers from measured equivalence.

teaching_path.action: Change to CH4 as an independent test.
teaching_path.why_valid: Equivalent C-H bonds coexist with four local directions and an sp3 model.
inputs: Only nitrate's three-direction planar framework supports the local sp2 description here.
teaching_path.output: The rejected equivalence-only rule fails a fresh fourth case.

teaching_path.action: Count sigma components by atom connectivity.

teaching_path.action: Count the extra components of the triple bond.

teaching_path.action: Reconcile local and whole-molecule inventories.
teaching_path.why_valid: The triple bond connects one neighbour at either end even though it has three components.

teaching_path.action: Specify the axial C-C sigma reference in both molecules.

inputs: Compare rotation about the central C–C bond in ethane with twisting about the C=C bond in ethene. Use the sigma and pi overlap arrangements to explain which overlap is altered by each motion. Do not infer a numerical energy barrier from a sketch.
teaching_path.output: A sigma connection can persist during torsion.

teaching_path.action: Identify the extra ethene pi alignment requirement.
teaching_path.why_valid: Its parallel residual p functions overlap laterally; relative group twist changes that alignment.
inputs: A sigma connection can persist during torsion.
teaching_path.output: Ethene twist alters pi overlap; ethane has no corresponding C-C pi component.

teaching_path.action: Separate rigid rotation from relative torsion.
teaching_path.why_valid: Only relative orientation about the bond changes the participating p relation.
inputs: Ethene twist alters pi overlap; ethane has no corresponding C-C pi component.
teaching_path.output: Rotating the whole molecule does not reproduce twisting one group.

teaching_path.action: Bound the energy inference.
teaching_path.why_valid: Other interactions, including hyperconjugation, can change even when the central sigma connection remains.
inputs: Rotating the whole molecule does not reproduce twisting one group.
teaching_path.output: No numerical barrier or exclusively steric total-energy law follows from the sketch.

teaching_path.action: Trace consecutive p-bearing carbon sites in butadiene.

teaching_path.action: Trace the second molecule using the same local test.
teaching_path.why_valid: Its intervening saturated CH2 uses localized sp3 accounting, with no ordinary residual p in this model.
inputs: A four-site contiguous aligned p pathway.
teaching_path.output: The central spacer interrupts the contiguous pathway.

teaching_path.action: Distinguish adjacency from spatial proximity.

inputs: The ordinary through-chain conjugation criterion remains unmet.

items.title: Axial chirality in substituted allenes from orthogonal pi planes
items.prompt: Penta-2,3-diene, CH3–CH=C=CH–CH3, possesses no asymmetric tetrahedral carbon atom, yet it is a chiral molecule that can be resolved into two non-superimposable enantiomers. Using the orthogonal pi-bonding framework of allene, explain the stereochemical origin of this axial chirality. What would happen to chirality if allene were planar?
items.source_label: Original competition-style transfer problem on allene axial chirality; not claimed as an official past-paper exam question.

answer.summary: The perpendicular orientation of the terminal groups creates a chiral C2-symmetric propeller that lacks any plane or centre of symmetry when each terminal carbon carries two different substituents (–H and –CH3). If allene were planar, the entire molecule would possess a plane of symmetry (the molecular plane) and would be strictly achiral.
reasoning: In penta-2,3-diene, central C3 is sp hybridised with orthogonal py and pz orbitals.
This forces the C2–H(CH3) plane and C4–H(CH3) plane to lie at 90° to each other.
Because each terminal carbon carries two distinct groups (H ≠ CH3), the orthogonal arrangement destroys all planes of symmetry (σ) and inversion centres (i), generating axial chirality.
If allene were planar, all atoms would lie in a single reflection plane, making enantiomerism impossible.

items.title: Heats of hydrogenation and resonance stabilization in conjugated vs non-conjugated dienes
items.prompt: The heat of hydrogenation of penta-1,4-diene is approximately -254 kJ/mol (nearly double that of 1-pentene, -126 kJ/mol). In contrast, the heat of hydrogenation of buta-1,3-diene is -239 kJ/mol, which is about 15 kJ/mol less exothermic than expected for two isolated double bonds. Explain this thermodynamic difference in terms of continuous p-orbital overlap versus structural interruption by an sp³ carbon.
items.source_label: Original competition-style transfer problem on diene thermodynamic stability; not claimed as an official past-paper exam question.

answer.summary: Buta-1,3-diene has continuous parallel p-orbital overlap across all four carbons, creating a delocalised 4-centre pi molecular orbital that provides ~15 kJ/mol of resonance/conjugation stabilization energy (lowering the enthalpy of the diene). Penta-1,4-diene has an intervening sp³ methylene carbon that breaks orbital continuity, leaving two completely isolated double bonds that release the full, additive heat of two independent alkene hydrogenations.
reasoning: In buta-1,3-diene, contiguous sp² carbons permit continuous pi electron delocalisation, lowering the ground-state enthalpy by the resonance energy (~15 kJ/mol).
Hydrogenation releases less heat because the starting material is already thermodynamically stabilized.
In penta-1,4-diene, the saturated sp³ C3 carbon has no available p orbital, completely insulating the two pi bonds so no delocalisation energy exists.
